newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian fishermen block Alaska ferry in salmon war.
newsitem.headline: Canadian fishermen block Alaska ferry in salmon war.

text.p: About 200 fishing boats surrounded an Alaskan ferry on Saturday in this British Columbia port, demanding progress in a salmon fishing dispute between Canada and the United States.

Spokesmen for the United Fishermen and Allied Workers union and ferry operator Alaska Marine Highway said the ferry was allowed to make its regular port call into Prince Rupert at 6 a.m. PDT (1300 GMT) to let off about 300 passengers and some vehicles.
But they said angry Canadian fishermen then anchored their boats behind the ferry, blocking its departure, and blockaded a convoy of trucks carrying salmon from leaving the ferry.
Union vice president Jim Sinclair said the union had not organised the action and did not know how long the ferry would be trapped in Prince Rupert.

"This is something that has taken on a life of its own," Sinclair said. "The Americans are stealing fish from Canadians here, stealing their livelihoods. Up to $5 million of fish have been taken that's not theirs," St. Clair told the Canadian Press news agency.

Murray Sheppard, the Alaska Marine Highway terminal manager in Prince Rupert could not say whether the company would send another of its three ferries to call at Prince Rupert, but that one was scheduled to dock there at 8 p.m. PDT (0300 GMT) Sunday.
U.S. officials denied Canadian allegations on Friday that the United States was breaching an international treaty by overfishing salmon in the Pacific Ocean.
"We do not believe we are in violation of this treaty," a State Department official said.

Canada sent a diplomatic note to the State Department on Friday, accusing the United States of failing to live up to its obligations under a 1985 Pacific salmon treaty, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said in Ottawa.
U.S. officials confirmed the note had been received, but there was no immediate reply.

Canada's Fisheries Minister, David Anderson said Alaskan fishermen had caught about 350,000 Canada-bound sockeye salmon so far in the 1997 season -- an increase of 300 percent from the average of previous years.
The Canadian Press news agency reported that premier Glen Clark and British Columbia fishermen called on Anderson to intervene in the dispute.
Anderson said Saturday he will be in Prince Rupert Monday and Tuesday to speak to the fishermen.
U.S. officials say Alaskan fishermen always catch some sockeye along with the pink salmon they are entitled to catch, because the two species run together.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Friday that the 1997 stock was quite abundant and that the catch of both pink salmon and sockeye salmon had been quite high.

"The ratio of pink salmon to sockeye so far this season is consistent with the ratio of every year of the last five years," Burns said, adding there was "no deliberate attempt by the state of Alaska or by Alaskan fishermen to somehow go after sockeye salmon, which violate or exceed the ratio that has been in effect for five years."
Canada and the United States have been holding sporadic talks for months on how to divide Pacific salmon stocks but failed to reach agreement before this year's season started.
